targets.oldText: Use four fictionalised source cards whose approved dates are printed clearly. Read the date label and locator before reading the event summary. Place the earliest card first, then check each neighbouring pair by date. Add one arrow labelled ‘before’ or ‘after’; do not add ‘caused’ unless the approved source establishes a relationship. Next read a separate approved resilience profile. Underline the belief, value, practice or community support named by that source, identify the hardship or change described there, and write a bounded sentence: ‘In this supplied account, the source presents __ as one support.’ Add the limit that another person or account may describe support differently. Keep the timeline evidence and resilience account in separate columns before making one cautious connection. Create a rights and protest timeline from the supplied school-approved event cards. Retain every date label and source locator, order at least six cards, justify two neighbouring positions, and mark any dating uncertainty. Write two chronology statements that say before, after or during the same period without inventing causation. Then analyse two supplied belief-and-resilience profiles. For each, identify the belief, value, practice or community support actually named, the change or hardship in the source, and one way the source presents that support as helping. Compare one similarity or difference while preserving each account's words and limits. Finish with an evidence audit: one secure ordering decision, one causal claim you rejected because chronology was insufficient, one bounded resilience statement, and one question awaiting an authorised source check. Work may be pointed, sorted, signed, spoken, typed or exactly scribed. The lesson needs no personal or family disclosure. Every event card keeps its supplied date label and source locator; an uncertain date stays marked uncertain rather than being guessed. Chronology answers what came before and after, but order alone does not prove that one event caused another. A school-approved profile can describe how a named belief, value, practice or community support is presented as helping in hardship without claiming this is true for every person. No learner has to disclose a personal belief, protest experience, family history, identity, hardship or coping strategy.
